title: Merit is no merit (section 19)
hookLine: merit is called merit because it is no fixed thing

lines: A PUNCH CARD, A STAR CHART.
cards: A paper punch card sits in a wallet, nine holes punched, one to go. A child's chore chart on the fridge is crowded with gold stars. An app counts your steps and throws confetti at the goal.
We like a tally; there's a pleasure in watching the good add up. Buddhist life has its own word for the good that adds up, and it's an important one: merit.
Section nineteen of the Diamond Sutra picks that word up, turns it over once, and sets it down differently.

teach.b: First, the word. Merit, in Sanskrit punya, in Pali puñña, is the good that comes from good deeds: giving, keeping precepts, honoring teachers, meditating. In Buddhist communities it's a real and living idea.
People give food to monks, light lamps, sponsor a reading, speak of the merit of it, and sometimes share that merit with those who have died.
The Diamond Sutra doesn't throw any of that away; it comes back to merit again and again. Second, the question.
Once more, a gift on a staggering scale: someone fills a whole vast world system with the seven precious things and gives it all away. Much merit? Very much, Subhuti says.
Third, the turn, section nineteen's surprise in one sentence.

If merit were a real, solid thing, the Buddha says, the Tathagata would not call it much merit; it's because merit is no fixed thing that he calls it much. The merit isn't denied. Its size isn't denied.
What's taken away is the idea that it's a thing you can stack, own, and carry in a pocket. Fourth, the lightness. Some readers hear relief in this.
If merit were a pile, you'd have to guard it, compare it, worry about losing it.
Because it's so-called merit, a name for the way good spreads out, there's nothing to guard.
You can do good and let it go, the way a river doesn't keep the water it passes on. The good is still good. It just isn't yours to count.

how: In Buddhist communities people make merit by giving to monks and nuns, keeping precepts and supporting teaching, and some dedicate or share that merit with others; Mahayana teachers read section 19 as a reminder not to cling to merit as a possession.

games.q: what does “merit is no merit” mean?
o: merit is real, but no fixed thing to stack, own or count
merit is a reward only monks are able to earn
merit is fake, so good deeds don't matter at all

p: a world filled with seven treasures
if merit were a real thing

s: the Diamond Sutra says merit doesn't matter
it calls the merit much; it only denies that merit is a fixed thing to own.
section 19 says merit is called much because it is no fixed thing
if it were a real, solid thing, the Tathagata wouldn't call it much.
Subhuti says the giver of a world of treasure gains little

games.q: you're Subhuti. someone gives away a whole world filled with seven treasures. the Buddha asks: much merit? what do you say?
o: only if they tell no one
games.why: Subhuti says very much, and the Buddha explains: it's called much because merit is no fixed thing.

practice: Bring to mind a kindness someone did for you that you never paid back, a ride, a meal, a word at the right moment, and notice the pull to balance it, to owe, to even things up.

No need to fight that pull; just see it, and let the kindness stay unbalanced, a gift that was never a transaction. Breathe in, receiving it; breathe out, letting it pass through you toward someone you haven't met yet.

wordCard.voice: Merit is no merit. Section nineteen says the Tathagata calls merit much precisely because it is no fixed thing. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: merit, the good that comes from good deeds; Pali puñña.

carryVoice: Your line: so-called merit. Good that spreads out, with nothing to guard. That's today, done.
